You will also provide a full answer from the content you have available. Use the data provided to generate follow-up queries to help refine your search. Do not ask compound questions, for example: "What is the market cap of Apple and Microsoft?". Use your knowledge of the entity distribution to focus on entity types that will be useful for searching a broad area of the knowledge graph.

For the query:

During a cross-host redirect, trace the decision to remove an Authorization header and identify the condition for replacing auth from the environment.

The top-ranked community summaries:

# Requests Session Authentication Redirect Controls

This community centers on the externally defined Requests session API and its authentication-related redirect behavior. Multiple tests create requests.Session objects and exercise should_strip_auth across host changes, HTTP downgrades, HTTPS upgrades, port changes, and equivalent default ports. The rebuild_auth routine uses that decision to remove Authorization headers and may reapply netrc credentials under trusted environment settings. The available evidence also shows session certificate configuration and a parametrized test fixture. The implementation of the external Session class and the runtime binding of should_strip_auth are not visible, so the findings primarily describe tested behavior and documented call relationships rather than independently verified production behavior.

## Requests Session is the central integration point

REQUESTS.SESSION is the central entity connecting the redirect-authentication tests and session configuration. The available description identifies requests.Session() and requests.session() as externally provided mechanisms for creating persistent HTTP sessions used with headers, cookies, proxies, redirect handling, TLS-related settings, adapters, and authentication workflows [Data: Entities (32); Relationships (2110, 2111, 2112, 2136, 40)].

The evidence does not expose the implementation of the Session class or prove every runtime binding described by the tests. Accordingly, the community demonstrates extensive interaction with the Requests session interface, but not independent verification of the external library's internal implementation [Data: Entities (32); Relationships (2110, 2111, 2112, 2136, 40)].

## Authentication is evaluated during redirect transitions

REBUILD_AUTH is defined to reconstruct request authentication. When an Authorization header is present, it calls should_strip_auth with the original and destination URLs; when new credentials are available, it applies them through prepared_request.prepare_auth(new_auth) [Data: Entities (789); Relationships (1056, 1066)].

This makes redirect URL comparison a security-relevant control point: the result of should_strip_auth determines whether existing authentication is removed before the redirected request proceeds. The available evidence supports this control flow, while the implementations of prepare_auth and the receiver-qualified should_strip_auth method remain unresolved in the supplied context [Data: Entities (789, 793); Relationships (1056, 1066)].

## Host changes are tested as requiring authentication stripping

The host-change test constructs a Requests session and asserts that should_strip_auth returns true when redirecting from http://example.com/foo to http://another.example.com/ [Data: Entities (1290); Relationships (2110)].

This test indicates that a change in host is treated as a boundary at which authentication should not automatically be carried forward. The record establishes the asserted behavior and the Session constructor call, but it does not establish how credentials are stored, whether the test passes in every supported version, or how other authentication mechanisms behave [Data: Entities (1290, 32); Relationships (2110)].

## Protocol and port changes receive differentiated treatment

The test community distinguishes among redirect types. HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade is asserted to strip authentication, while HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrade is asserted not to strip authentication in standard-port cases; the upgrade test description also states that non-standard ports should trigger stripping. A separate test asserts stripping for a transition from http://example.com:1234/foo to https://example.com:4321/bar [Data: Entities (1291, 1292, 1294); Relationships (2111, 2112, 2136)].

These records show that the intended policy is not simply 'strip on every scheme change.' It considers scheme direction and port identity, with downgrade and port changes treated more restrictively than equivalent standard-port upgrades [Data: Entities (1291, 1292, 1294); Relationships (2111, 2112, 2136)].

## Equivalent default ports are explicitly covered

The parametrized default-port test asserts that should_strip_auth is false for equivalent default HTTP and HTTPS ports. The test is parameterized through pytest.mark.parametrize over old and new URI pairs, indicating that multiple URI combinations are intended to be evaluated under the same assertion [Data: Entities (1295); Relationships (2138)].

This coverage is important because it separates semantically equivalent default-port representations from non-standard port changes. However, the supplied data does not list the concrete parameter values, so the exact URI combinations covered cannot be independently enumerated from the available records [Data: Entities (1295); Relationships (2138)].

## Session certificate configuration is connected to the same API surface

The evidence shows a write to Session.cert after a session is created: s.cert = '/path/client.cert'. The relationship identifies this as an attribute write from requests.Session to Session.cert, establishing that client-certificate configuration is part of the observed session usage [Data: Entities (48); Relationships (40)].

The owning class implementation and the operational effect of the certificate setting are not visible. Therefore, the evidence supports the existence of this configuration interaction but does not support conclusions about certificate validation, key protection, deployment practices, or compliance [Data: Entities (48); Relationships (40)].

## Evidence is test- and interface-oriented rather than operational

The supplied community is composed primarily of named tests, unresolved or externally defined API entities, and call/write relationships. The records establish assertions about redirect authentication behavior and references to Session APIs, but they provide no information about production deployment, users, organizations, legal compliance, reputation, incident history, or observed misuse [Data: Entities (1290, 1291, 1292, 1294, 1295); Relationships (2110, 2111, 2112, 2136, 2138)].

Consequently, the strongest supported assessment concerns the importance of authentication handling in the code path and the breadth of its test coverage. Any judgment about real-world exposure or actual security outcomes would require implementation, version, execution, and deployment evidence not included here [Data: Entities (32, 789, 793); Relationships (1056, 1066)].

# Digest Authentication Request-Handling Code Community

This community is centered on the `handle_401` and `__call__` methods, which form a request-authentication and response-hook workflow. `__call__` initializes per-thread state, optionally records the request-body position, and registers response hooks for authentication failures and redirects. `handle_401` recognizes qualifying Digest authentication challenges, constructs a new authorization header, rewinds the request body when possible, resends the request, and records the original response in the retry history. Supporting entities include unresolved request, connection, regular-expression, history, and authentication-header operations. A separate capability branch checks whether `requests.pyopenssl` is available and sets `HAS_PYOPENSSL` accordingly. The evidence describes technical behavior but does not establish the owning class, deployment context, legal compliance, reputation, or any confirmed misuse.

## Central role of `handle_401` in Digest authentication recovery

`handle_401` is the most connected entity in the community and coordinates the principal recovery path for qualifying 4xx responses. It compiles a case-insensitive Digest pattern, removes the Digest prefix from the authentication challenge, invokes `build_digest_header`, resends the prepared request, and appends the original response to the new response history [Data: Entities (437); Relationships (472, 475, 476, 485, 486)].

This makes `handle_401` the operational hub for authentication retry behavior. The owning class is not visible, and the runtime types of several receivers are unresolved, so the evidence supports the described call relationships but not conclusions about the broader application or its security posture.

## `__call__` establishes the request-processing hook workflow

`__call__` unconditionally initializes per-thread state before inspecting the request. It may record the request body's current position, catches `AttributeError` when that operation is unavailable, and registers `handle_401` and `handle_redirect` as response hooks [Data: Entities (438, 448, 449); Relationships (477, 479, 480, 482, 487)].

The method therefore links request preparation with later response handling. The data shows hook registration rather than immediate execution of the handlers, and it does not identify the request object's concrete implementation.

## Request-body rewind supports authentication retries

The workflow attempts to preserve a body position through `r.body.tell()` and later uses `r.request.body.seek(self._thread_local.pos)` in `handle_401` when a saved position exists [Data: Entities (442, 448); Relationships (479, 488)].

This behavior is technically significant because resending a request may require restoring a consumable body. The evidence also shows that missing or incompatible body interfaces are expected: `AttributeError` is caught when position tracking is unavailable [Data: Entities (454); Relationships (487)]. No evidence establishes whether every body type can be safely rewound or whether retry limits beyond the described path exist.

## Authentication retry depends on unresolved header-construction and connection operations

After detecting a qualifying Digest challenge, `handle_401` calls the unresolved `build_digest_header` method with the prepared request method and URL, then sends the prepared request through `r.connection.send(prep, **kwargs)` [Data: Entities (437, 441, 446); Relationships (475, 476)].

These dependencies are important control points in the community, but their implementations and owning classes are absent. Consequently, the supplied evidence confirms orchestration of header generation and retransmission without supporting claims about credential storage, cryptographic strength, transport protection, or connection security.

## Redirect handling modifies per-thread retry state

`handle_redirect` checks `r.is_redirect` and, when true, writes `1` to `self._thread_local.num_401_calls` [Data: Entities (436); Relationships (482)]. The method is registered by `__call__` as a response hook, establishing a relationship between redirect processing and the thread-local state used by the authentication workflow [Data: Entities (438); Relationships (480, 482)].

The available records do not describe the complete retry-state lifecycle or show how this value affects subsequent requests. The evidence therefore supports a state-reset or state-update function but not a definitive assessment of loop prevention or redirect security.

## PyOpenSSL availability is represented as a capability flag

`HAS_PYOPENSSL` is assigned based on whether the external `requests.pyopenssl` attribute can be accessed: an `AttributeError` results in `False`, while successful access results in `True` [Data: Entities (1075, 1077); Relationships (1624)].

The same compatibility-oriented exception handling pattern appears elsewhere, including netrc authentication, body operations, length calculation, cookie merging, and authentication lookup [Data: Entities (454)]. The data indicates capability detection and fallback handling, but it does not show which downstream features consume the flag or whether PyOpenSSL is actually used at runtime.

## The community is technically interconnected but contextually incomplete

The highest-degree entities are `handle_401` and `__call__`, while most supporting operations are low-degree unresolved references such as `BUILD_DIGEST_HEADER`, `R.CONNECTION.SEND`, `R.BODY.SEEK`, and `R.REGISTER_HOOK` [Data: Entities (437, 438, 441, 442, 446, +more)]. The relationship records show a coherent request-authentication pipeline connecting these symbols [Data: Relationships (472, 475, 476, 477, 479, +more)].

However, the provided records contain no ownership, organization, legal, reputation, incident, or deployment information. Any assessment beyond the documented code behavior would require additional evidence identifying the owning class, package version, execution environment, and relevant operational or compliance records.

{"intermediate_answer":"# Redirect Authentication Decision

The supplied evidence places the decision in `rebuild_auth`, which reconstructs authentication during a redirect. When the redirected request already has an `Authorization` header, `rebuild_auth` calls `should_strip_auth` with the original URL and the destination URL [Data: Entities (789); Relationships (1056)]. If that decision is true, the existing header is removed before the redirected request continues. Thus, the direct trace is: redirect processing invokes `rebuild_auth`; `rebuild_auth` compares the two URLs through `should_strip_auth`; a true result causes the `Authorization` header to be stripped.

The strongest explicitly supported trigger is a host change. The test for `http://example.com/foo` to `http://another.example.com/` asserts that `should_strip_auth` returns true [Data: Entities (1290); Relationships (2110)]. Authentication is also stripped for an HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade and for a change involving non-equivalent ports, such as `http://example.com:1234/foo` to `https://example.com:4321/bar` [Data: Entities (1291, 1294); Relationships (2111, 2136)]. The policy is differentiated rather than stripping on every scheme change: an HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrade can retain authentication for equivalent standard ports, and equivalent default-port cases are asserted not to strip [Data: Entities (1292, 1295); Relationships (2112, 2138)].

After the old header is removed, the environment-based replacement condition is that trusted-environment handling is enabled and netrc lookup supplies new credentials. The summary describes `rebuild_auth` as potentially reapplying netrc credentials under trusted environment settings, using `prepared_request.prepare_auth(new_auth)` when new credentials are available [Data: Entities (789); Relationships (1066)]. In operational terms supported by the snapshot, replacement therefore requires `trust_env` to permit environment credential lookup and a nonempty netrc result (`new_auth`); the new credentials are then passed to `prepare_auth`.

Important uncertainty remains. The supplied records do not expose the `Session` implementation, the runtime binding of `should_strip_auth`, the exact netrc lookup code, or the concrete definition of `trust_env`. They establish tested behavior and documented call relationships, not independently verified production execution. The evidence also does not show what happens when netrc lookup returns no credentials beyond indicating that replacement requires credentials to be available.
